intro: Two hands share a stream of repeated notes; chromatic lines and displaced accents keep changing what those notes mean. Martha Argerich plays the Toccata Prokofiev wrote while he was still a St Petersburg Conservatory student.
question: How can repeated notes keep changing their weight and direction?

sections.label: Quiet restart
sections.mNote: repeated-note mechanism returns with reduced weight

sections.label: D-centred return
sections.mNote: repeated Ds return in heavier octaves across both hands

cues.title: One note, two hands
cues.text: The opening shares repeated Ds between the hands before chromatic neighbours widen the pitch field. Listen for the distinction between the running semiquavers and the accents laid across them: regular small notes can carry shifting emphasis.
cues.evidence: The score specifies the repeated-note opening. D dominates the report’s first 25 seconds, with frequent attacks; this supports the opening span, not an exact note alignment.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A classmate’s fingers
cues.text: Prokofiev dedicated the Toccata to Nikolay Shtember, his fellow pupil in Anna Esipova’s piano class at the St Petersburg Conservatory. Written in spring 1912, it tested Shtember’s technique and the composer’s own.
cues.evidence: Simon Morrison documents the dedication and composition in the Henle HN 1581 preface, pp. IV–V: https://www.henle.de/media/7f/27/66/1708068498/1581.pdf

cues.title: Seventy-five roubles
cues.text: Koussevitzky’s publishing firm rejected the Toccata. Jurgenson offered fifty roubles; Prokofiev negotiated seventy-five, then complained about delayed proofs. The first edition appeared in July 1913.
cues.evidence: Morrison’s Henle preface, p. IV, documents the fees and publication history, citing Prokofiev’s diary: https://www.henle.de/media/7f/27/66/1708068498/1581.pdf

cues.title: Less weight, continued movement
cues.text: This stretch reduces the weight of the repeated-note writing without replacing it with a slow song. Compare the quieter attacks with the force of the preceding passage.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls sharply around 1:40 and again near 1:50 while frequent attacks continue. The measurement supports the contrast across the passage.

cues.title: Follow movement underneath
cues.text: As the sound grows heavier again, follow the changing lower notes beneath the repeated attacks. The underlying line can move while the surface keeps its persistent rhythmic pattern.
cues.evidence: The report shows a stronger span around 2:10–2:25 and changing low-pitch estimates. It does not establish a chord-by-chord harmonic analysis.

cues.title: A restrained American debut
cues.text: At his American debut in the Brooklyn Museum on 29 October 1918, Prokofiev played the Toccata before a reception for an exhibition of Boris Anisfeld’s work. Simon Morrison’s account describes him softening its impact for that audience, even leaving notes out.
cues.evidence: Morrison’s Henle preface, p. V, describes the occasion and cites the Brooklyn Daily Eagle review of 30 October 1918: https://www.henle.de/media/7f/27/66/1708068498/1581.pdf

cues.title: The opening pitch returns
cues.text: In the later D-centred stretch, compare the recurring pitch with its quieter opening role. A fixed note can become a reference point even when neighbouring notes keep pressing against it.
cues.evidence: D dominates both the opening and the span around 3:20–3:35, at a higher relative level later. The score supplies the repeated-note comparison; the key labels alone are not treated as proof.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A break in the stream
cues.text: The closing stretch includes a marked withdrawal before a final burst. Listen for the contrast between sparse attacks and the continuous motion that has occupied much of the piece.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls around 3:35–3:45, and detected attacks become sparse by 3:45, before renewed activity around 3:50–3:55. No exact interruption second is claimed.

cues.title: The last burst and decay
cues.text: Near the end, the repeated attacks make one more concentrated burst. Listen beyond the final attack to the resonance that remains after the rhythmic stream has stopped.
cues.evidence: The report shows high relative level and frequent attacks around 3:55, followed by a sharp retreat around 4:00 and near silence by 4:05. The final keystroke is not precisely timed.

transitions.title: The repeated note survives the withdrawal
transitions.how: After the chromatic writing has expanded the opening’s narrow pitch field, the repeated-note idea reappears with much less weight. D remains the reference point; the change is not a cadence into a contrasting lyrical key. The hands continue sharing rapid attacks while their dynamic shrinks, so the pulse persists underneath the withdrawal. That separation of speed from force prepares another expansion: quiet here means the same mechanism heard with less pressure, not a slow movement inserted into it.
transitions.evidence: The 1:40 section boundary is a strong analysis change: level falls from about −4.6 dB at 1:35 to −16.2 dB at 1:40 and −29.1 dB at 1:50, while frequent attacks and D-centred pitch content continue. The score’s recurrent repeated-note material, described in the existing cues and the published Toccata work account, supplies the connection; no new key is inferred from a five-second estimate.

transitions.title: Chromatic travel contracts onto D
transitions.how: The preceding passage drives chromatic lines in opposite directions and brings the descending-third material back around D. Prokofiev then contracts that travelling harmony onto repeated D octaves, now exchanged by both hands rather than tapped out with the opening’s relative thinness. The widened register and heavier attack make the pitch unmistakable, but a bare D octave does not establish a D-major or D-minor chord. Recognition comes through the repeated-note rhythm and its tonal centre, not a conventional dominant–tonic cadence.
transitions.evidence: The 3:22 section boundary is a strong change; low-pitch estimates move from A near 3:15 to D around 3:20, with D prominent thereafter. The score description in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_(Prokofiev) identifies the chromatic contrary motion, descending-third material in D and return of repeated D in alternating octaves. The relation file supplies no independent formal-reprise alignment.

transitions.title: A stopped pulse becomes a final climb
transitions.how: The repeated octaves slow and the continuous stream finally breaks. When motion resumes, repeated notes turn into a rising chromatic line, followed by emphatic octaves and an upward glissando. The ending answers that climb with two sforzando D octaves at opposite ends of the keyboard. There is no need for a new theme or a full closing triad: the note that began the piece now occupies the extremes of its register, after the interruption has made its renewed attack conspicuous.
transitions.evidence: The 3:50 section boundary follows the sparse 3:35–3:45 withdrawal; level rises from about −27.8 dB at 3:45 to −4.4 dB at 3:55, when attack density reaches 7.2 per second. The published score description identifies the slowdown, halt, chromatic ascent, glissando and final D octaves. The span covers that sequence without assigning exact seconds to its individual gestures.

quote.text: It seemed to me that if Haydn had lived in our day he would have retained his own style while accepting something of the new at the same time.
quote.source: Autobiography, explaining the Classical Symphony of 1917

composer.background:
Prokofiev grew up on the Sontsovka estate in Ukraine, where his father managed the agricultural business and his mother played Beethoven and Chopin at the piano. He remembered hearing sonatas from another room after being put to bed. The keyboard was therefore familiar before the concert hall: his mother wrote down his first pieces, and a visit to Moscow opera performances in 1900 prompted the nine-year-old to compose The Giant for performance at home. Sergei Taneyev subsequently recommended professional instruction. Reinhold Glière spent the summers of 1902 and 1903 at Sontsovka, teaching composition and helping the boy turn his accumulating pieces into larger forms.

He entered the St Petersburg Conservatory at thirteen, bringing manuscripts of his compositions. Rimsky-Korsakov taught orchestration, Anatoly Lyadov harmony and counterpoint, Nikolai Tcherepnin conducting, and Anna Esipova piano. Tcherepnin’s attention to Haydn and Mozart mattered as much as the harmonic experiments Prokofiev pursued outside class. Nikolai Myaskovsky, an older fellow student, became a lifelong correspondent and a critic whose objections he took seriously. Their correspondence continued to test decisions about form and orchestration long after the Conservatory.
composer.born: 23 April 1891, Sontsovka, Ukraine, then Russian Empire
composer.epithet: A pianist who made the keyboard strike like percussion, and a theatre composer whose longest melodies keep their footing through abrupt changes of key.
